reporting_issues.note: Abstract (p. 136) gives 50.4%; the Discussion (p. 139) uses the cumulative figures. The Conclusion (p. 141) gives a range, one-third to one-half, that names neither figure, so 'use only the second' is exact for the abstract and the Discussion and an inference for the Conclusion.
p. 138, 3.2.1, 1st paragraph (no onset data beyond 14 years for STUD; right-censored there) and 3.3 ('lifetime cumulative probability' within an estimated 14 years).
p. 137: the five-uses rule (2.1, 2nd paragraph) and the subsample definition (2.1, 1st paragraph) are never connected.

The two rules apply to different respondents: 2.1 bottom-codes reported exact ages below 14 at 13, while 2.2 codes the answers of people who could not recall an exact age (before their teens 12, before their twenties 19, after their twenties 20). They do not conflict; they code comparable answers inconsistently (an exact age of 11 becomes 13, 'before the teens' becomes 12). Suggested issue: 'Age of first use is coded by different rules for exact ages (under 14 coded 13; 2.1) and for recall-probe answers (12, 19 or 20; 2.2), so comparable answers are coded differently.' Consequence as on the card.

Recomputed: 579/8,841 = 6.5%; 5,456/8,841 = 61.7%; 3.3/0.457 = 7.2%, 22.1/0.345 = 64.1%, 6.2/0.318 = 19.5%; also sedatives 0.6/0.390 = 1.5% against 137/8,841 = 1.5% and opioids 0.9/0.447 = 2.0% against 1.8%, which supports the reading as weighted prevalence of the disorder. The hedge ('probably') is appropriate.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence matches the design (survey). Overall moderate agreed: a national probability survey with a standard interview; the limits for this encyclopedia are the undefined class, abuse in the outcome, recalled timing and the ambiguous denominator, as the reasoning says.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: With reporting issue 3 reworded, 'inconsistent rules' remains accurate.
See missed: the 14-year projection also rests on assumptions the paper does not discuss.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed. The abstract's 'would develop' frames a model projection as a forecast and ranks substances that the limitations say cannot be compared directly, but the headline numbers are reported as computed and the Discussion concedes that counting abuse raises them.

missed: The 14-year cumulative probability (p. 138) assumes that people who started using recently will pass to a disorder at the same yearly rates as those who started earlier (no change across birth cohorts or periods) and that censoring at the interview is uninformative; the later years after first use are informed only by people who started long ago, whose ages of first use and onset were recalled over longer spans. The paper does not discuss this, and it is part of why 50.4% exceeds the descriptive 45.7%.
